drafts/harbourline--storefront-128/revie.title: Paginate the orders endpoint
drafts/harbourline--storefront-128/revie.summary: Page one starts at the twenty sixth order, and the query stopped asking whose orders these are.
drafts/harbourline--storefront-128/revie.comment:
**Start here.** This is the interface, running, with a review loaded into it. Nothing on this page is a picture. The summary above is the agent's; click it to write your own.

On the left is everything the agent looked through, the lenses that came back clean included. Click one and the review filters to it. Open **Query cost** to see what a clean lens is for. The **Diff** tab hangs these same cards under the lines they are about, and the **QA** tab plays the run that failed.

Drop a finding you disagree with and it stops being part of the review. Reload the page and it is still dropped, because your decisions are an append-only log rather than a page of state. **Post review**, bottom right, is where a real review would leave. Here it goes nowhere and says so.

**Request changes.** Paging this endpoint is overdue and the shape of the change is right. Two lines of it are not.

The `where` clause went missing in the rewrite, so the query now returns the newest orders in the shop rather than the newest orders belonging to whoever asked. That is every customer's address, basket and total, served to anybody with an account.

The offset is one page out. `page * limit` on page one skips the first twenty five orders, so a customer who has just checked out cannot find the order they placed a minute ago. The test that ships with the change passes either way.

sections.label: Who sees what
sections.body: The query is the only thing that decides whose orders come back. `requireCustomer` above it proves somebody is signed in and says nothing about which rows they may read.

sections.label: Correctness
sections.body: The paging arithmetic, and what a caller actually gets for the page they asked for.

sections.label: Limits
sections.body: What one request can ask this endpoint to do, and what stops it.

sections.label: Tests
sections.body: The change ships a test with it, which is the rule here. What that test pins down is the question.

sections.label: The response
sections.body: What the client is handed, and what it is left to work out for itself.

sections.label: Query cost
sections.body:
Clean, and worth showing rather than hiding.

Worth checking because paging is where one query usually becomes one query per row: the page comes back and then something gets looked up for each item on it.

Checked: `summarise` reads `total`, `placedAt` and `state` off the row it is handed and touches no relation, so it issues nothing. `findMany` is called once. `placedAt` is the sort column and carries an index, so `skip` and `take` walk a range rather than sorting the table to find the page.

**A lens with nothing flagged is the most useful thing on the page.** Leaving it out would make this review look shorter and make its thoroughness unprovable. Checked and clean, and not looked at, are different answers.

findings.body:
The `where` clause did not move in the rewrite. It is gone.

`findMany` now filters on nothing, so this returns the twenty five newest orders in the shop. `requireCustomer` only proves somebody is signed in. Any account can now read any other customer's order: the delivery address, the line items and the total, all of which `summarise` returns.

The old query had one condition and that condition carried the whole rule. Nothing else in the request path applies it, which is why taking it out breaks no existing test.

Fix this one first. The offset below is wrong in a way a customer notices. This one is wrong in a way they do not.

`page` is one based on the line above: the default is `1`, and the response echoes it back. The offset treats it as zero based.

So `?page=1` skips twenty five orders and answers with the twenty sixth onwards. The newest order on the account cannot be reached through this endpoint at all, except by asking for `?page=0`, which nothing tells a client to do.

The customer who meets this is the one who has just checked out and gone looking for their order.

`limit` comes off the query string and goes into `take` unread. `?limit=1000000` reads the table and serialises it, and any signed in account can send that.

`Number` is the only thing between the two, so `?limit=abc` reaches the driver as `NaN` and `?limit=-1` reaches it as a negative `take`. What those two do is worth knowing before this ships rather than after.

A ceiling is the whole fix, and it belongs on this line rather than in the query.

Sixty orders, page one, twenty five back. That is true with the offset as written and true with the offset fixed, because both return a full page. It is also true when the rows belong to somebody else, because it counts them and never looks at them.

The test that would have caught both findings is the same size as this one: seed the orders, ask for page one, assert the first entry is the newest order by id. It fails today.

The other boundary is worth a line too. Sixty orders in pages of twenty five means the last page holds ten, and nothing here says what happens past it.

A question rather than a blocker.

The response carries the page it served and the rows on it. It does not carry how many rows there are, so a client cannot say "page 3 of 7", cannot grey out a next button, and finds the end by asking for a page and getting an empty one.

That may be exactly what you want. A count is a second query on every request, and a screen that scrolls never needs one. But if the account page is getting numbered pages, it needs the count, and adding it once clients have been written against this shape is the awkward version of the change.

Which is it? Nothing to do here if the answer is scrolling.

qa.note:
Driven against a local shop seeded with sixty orders on one account and eleven on another. The run below is the failing one, and it is the point of this review: the first page of the account's orders does not contain the order that was just placed.

The access finding was not driven. It needs two signed in browsers to show, and it is provable from the diff without them, because the query has no condition left on it. Read instead: `requireCustomer`, which sets `request.customer` and asserts nothing about rows, and `summarise`, which returns the delivery address.

scenarios.what: the first page holds the order just placed

drafts/harbourline--storefront-131/revie.title: Round the order total once, at the end
drafts/harbourline--storefront-131/revie.summary: Rounds once and the arithmetic holds. Orders already placed keep the old penny, which matters to refunds.
drafts/harbourline--storefront-131/revie.comment:
**Approve.** Rounding every line and then adding them up is how a total ends up a penny above the invoice, and this is the fix: add the lines, apply the rate, round once.

One thing to carry away rather than to change here. Every order already in the database was totalled the old way, so recomputing one now can come out a penny from what the customer was actually charged. `refunds.js` recomputes. That is a separate pull request and it is worth writing.

sections.label: Arithmetic
sections.body:
Clean.

Checked: `Math.round` is half up on positives, and every price in this shop is positive, so the boundary rounds the way the invoice template rounds. The multiplication happens before the division, so what gets rounded is a whole number of pence and there is no second rounding hiding inside it. Nothing compares the result to another float with `===`: the only caller is `charge.js`, which sends it to the gateway as pence.

sections.label: Orders already placed
sections.body: A change to how a total is computed is a change to every total anybody recomputes, including the ones that were charged under the old arithmetic.

sections.label: The invoice
sections.body: What the customer is shown, and whether it still agrees with what this function returns.

sections.label: Tests
sections.body: The added test fails on the old code and passes on the new one, which is what makes it a test of this change rather than a description of it. Two lines at seven pence with tax at 8.25 per cent come to fifteen pence added together and sixteen rounded a line at a time.

findings.body:
Not a reason to hold this up. It is the thing to know about it.

Every order placed before this deploys was totalled a line at a time, and some of those totals are a penny above what this function now returns for the same basket. The number the customer was charged is the old one.

So anything that recomputes a total for an old order disagrees with what happened. `refunds.js` does exactly that: it calls `orderTotal(order.lines, order.taxRate)` rather than reading `order.total`, and a refund a penny short is a support ticket rather than a rounding detail.

Reading the stored total is the fix, and it is the right thing to do whether or not this lands. It belongs in its own pull request rather than growing this one.

A question, not a blocker.

`taxRate` was one number for the whole order before this change too, so the assumption is not new. What is new is that the rate is applied once to the sum, which makes the assumption load bearing in a way it was not when every line carried its own multiplication.

The invoice template prints a tax column per line. If a basket can ever mix rates, books at zero beside a bookmark at twenty, then the invoice and the total already disagree, and this shape makes that harder to unpick later.

If a basket is always one rate, say so in the signature and this is settled.

qa.note: Driven against a local shop with the basket from the bug report: two items at seven pence, tax at 8.25 per cent. The run below walks the basket, the checkout page and the confirmation, and all three say fifteen pence. On the old code the checkout page said sixteen and the gateway was sent fifteen.

scenarios.what: the total on the page is the amount charged

drafts/harbourline--storefront-134/revie.title: Export button does nothing
drafts/harbourline--storefront-134/revie.summary: The report is real and the ticket buries it. Reproduction, scope and the regression window are all in there, underneath the urgency.
drafts/harbourline--storefront-134/revie.description:
Orders export: "Export CSV" spins forever and no file downloads

Steps I took:
1. Signed in as the shop owner
2. Opened Orders
3. Clicked "Export CSV"
4. Waited a couple of minutes

The spinner just runs and runs and no file ever downloads.
I tried Chrome and Safari on my Mac and it is the same in both.

Expected: a CSV of the listed orders downloads within a few seconds.
Actual: the spinner runs until the page is reloaded; no file arrives.

It worked before last week's deploy, and month end reporting is blocked on it.
drafts/harbourline--storefront-134/revie.comment:
**This one is an issue, not a pull request.** There is no diff and no verdict, because there is no code to judge: the agent read the ticket instead, and what it proposes is a clearer ticket.

Open **Description** on the left. The proposal is not a comment saying "please clarify" - it is the rewritten body itself, cut into hunks against the ticket as it stands. Reject a hunk and the final body below recomputes without it; the reporter's own words win wherever you say so. Click the final body to write over the top of it.

When you post, the rewrite replaces the ticket's body and this comment goes underneath, so the reporter can see what changed and why. If someone edits the ticket while you are reading, posting refuses and rediffs rather than overwriting them.

Tidied the title into the symptom, kept your reproduction steps word for word, and moved the impact to where a triager will read it. Nothing was lost: the urgency is now the last line instead of the loudest one.

sections.label: The rewrite
sections.body:
What changed and why. The title now names the symptom, so the issue list reads as a list of symptoms rather than a list of alarm levels. The plea at the bottom became the two lines a fix gets measured against: expected and actual.

Each change is one hunk in the Description lens, and each stands or falls on its own.

sections.label: What the reporter got right
sections.body: Untouched, deliberately. The reproduction steps, the two browsers and the regression window are exactly what a fix needs, and they are in the reporter's own words in the middle of the ticket. A rewrite that restated them would be claiming their work; the hunks leave those lines alone, which you can check by reading what the diff does not touch.
